case: Maritime Delimitation and Territorial Questions between Qatar and Bahrain (Qatar v. Bahrain), Merits
parties: Qatar v. Bahrain
issue: Sovereignty over Hawar Islands, Zubarah, Janan, Qit'at Jaradah, Fasht ad Dibal; single maritime boundary. Bahrain relied on historic pearling banks north of Qatar as a special circumstance.
outcome: Hawar and Qit'at Jaradah to Bahrain; Zubarah, Janan and Fasht ad Dibal to Qatar; boundary adjusted. The Court did not treat the pearling banks as a reason to shift the line (paras about 235-236, wording to check). Qatar set aside 82 documents Bahrain challenged as not authentic.
how_checked: Date, holdings and the 82 documents checked on the ICJ judgment and press release. The pearling-banks paragraph could not be read online; paragraph numbers and wording are from memory and must be checked in the full text.
why_it_matters: The clearest case where old sea custom (pearling grounds worked by Bahraini divers) meets modern boundary law and loses. Also shows two Gulf rulers choosing a world court over GCC mediation, and the 1939 British decision being read as binding law.
paper_section: 3 (custom and pearling); 6 (sovereignty abroad); 8 (propositions on custom being replaced)

case: Qatar v. Bahrain, Jurisdiction and Admissibility (two judgments)
parties: Qatar v. Bahrain
citation: ICJ Reports 1994, p. 112; ICJ Reports 1995, p. 6
issue: Whether the 1987 letters and the 1990 Doha Minutes (signed at a GCC summit under Saudi mediation) were a binding agreement to go to the Court.
outcome: The Doha Minutes were held to be a binding international agreement; the Court took jurisdiction in 1995.
how_checked: 1994 judgment and the Doha Minutes ruling confirmed in secondary summary; 1995 date and citations from memory, check on ICJ case page.
why_it_matters: Minutes of a summit between rulers, with Saudi mediation, were turned into treaty law by a court. Shows personal and family diplomacy being translated into the form of international law.

case: Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, Advisory Opinion
parties: Request of UN General Assembly (res. 77/276); Saudi Arabia, UAE and Kuwait took part
issue: States' duties on climate change, including duties under UNCLOS to protect the marine environment.
outcome: Court found binding duties under treaties and custom, including UNCLOS. Oral statements: Saudi Arabia 2 Dec 2024, UAE 4 Dec 2024, Kuwait 6 Dec 2024. Qatar, Bahrain and Oman were not on the oral hearing list.
how_checked: Hearing schedule (Maastricht University programme of the ICJ hearings) and IISD Earth Negotiations Bulletin summary of statements.
why_it_matters: Three Gulf states speak in different registers in the same forum: Saudi Arabia defends the narrow treaty regime, the UAE (COP28 host) speaks of ambition, Kuwait offers its own national law as proof of good conduct. Good material on how each state presents itself abroad. Already in data/stance_records.csv.

court: International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea
case: Request for an Advisory Opinion submitted by the Commission of Small Island States on Climate Change and International Law (Case No. 31)
parties: COSIS request; Saudi Arabia made an oral statement on 13 Sept 2023 (Ms Noorah Mohammed Algethami); none of the six filed written statements
citation: ITLOS Case No. 31, Advisory Opinion of 21 May 2024
issue: Whether greenhouse gas emissions are marine pollution under UNCLOS Part XII.
outcome: Tribunal held that emissions are pollution of the marine environment and that UNCLOS duties apply. Saudi Arabia argued the climate treaties are lex specialis and the Tribunal should be restrained.
how_checked: ITLOS case page and verbatim record PV.23/C31/5 read.
why_it_matters: The only Gulf voice in the first ocean-climate case. Shows a state keeping the sea inside a negotiated treaty space it controls, and staying away from the written phase.

case: F4 environmental claims arising from Iraq's invasion and occupation of Kuwait
parties: Kuwait and Saudi Arabia (claimants) v. Iraq
citation: S/AC.26/Dec.258 (2005); F4 panel reports such as S/AC.26/2003/31
issue: Compensation for oil damage to the Gulf coast, intertidal zone and marine resources from the 1991 spills and oil fires.
outcome: Marine and coastal awards include: Saudi Arabia USD 463.3m (coastal remediation), 46.1m (intertidal compensatory project), 6.2m (marine); Kuwait 8.2m (oiled shoreline), 7.9m (shoreline compensation), 4.0m (marine and coastal). Decision 258 set up a follow-up programme and held back 15% until projects were finished.
why_it_matters: The largest body of legal decisions on Gulf marine damage. It set money values on coastal habitat and pushed both states to build environmental agencies and monitoring. A strong example of the sea's law being made outside the region and then taken home.

court: Ad hoc arbitration (sole arbitrator Lord Asquith of Bishopstone)
case: Petroleum Development (Trucial Coast) Ltd v. Sheikh of Abu Dhabi
parties: Petroleum Development (Trucial Coast) Ltd v. Sheikh Shakhbut of Abu Dhabi
issue: Whether a 1939 oil concession covered the seabed and continental shelf, a concept that did not exist when it was signed. Which law governs the concession.
outcome: The concession did not cover the continental shelf. The arbitrator refused to apply local law, saying in effect that the Sheikh's own law contained no settled rules for modern commercial contracts, and applied 'principles rooted in the good sense and common practice of civilised nations'.
how_checked: Existence, parties and citation confirmed on Cambridge ILR. Quoted wording is from memory; check against the ILR text.
why_it_matters: Founding moment for the sea-bed in Gulf law and a classic text on how outside lawyers dismissed Islamic and customary law. Ideal for the argument about law moving beyond the local, and about what was lost.

case: Petroleum Development (Qatar) Ltd v. Ruler of Qatar (1950); Ruler of Qatar v. International Marine Oil Co Ltd (1953)
parties: Ruler of Qatar; Petroleum Development (Qatar) Ltd; International Marine Oil Co
issue: Whether Qatar's onshore concession reached the seabed beyond territorial waters, so that the Ruler could grant an offshore concession to another company. Which law applies.
outcome: Offshore seabed was not part of the first concession, so the Ruler was free to grant it. In 1953 the arbitrator (Sir Alfred Bucknill) declined to apply Islamic law to the contract.
how_checked: Both reports found on Cambridge ILR. Arbitrator name and reasoning from memory; check ILR text.
why_it_matters: Same pattern as Abu Dhabi: the Ruler's sea became valuable and was framed through English and international law rather than Islamic law. Useful pair with INT-06 for the Qatar chapter.

case: Saudi Arabia v. Arabian American Oil Company (Aramco)
parties: Government of Saudi Arabia v. Aramco
issue: Whether Saudi Arabia could give a Greek shipowner (the Onassis tanker agreement, 1954) priority to carry Saudi oil by sea, against Aramco's concession rights.
outcome: Tribunal applied Saudi law, which it described as Hanbali Islamic law, but filled gaps with general principles and international law. Held for Aramco.
how_checked: Award listed on Trans-Lex with citation. Date and summary from memory and secondary sources; check the award text.
why_it_matters: A tribunal treats Hanbali fiqh as the law of the land but finds it silent on modern sea transport and concessions. Very good for how Islamic law is acknowledged and then set aside in maritime matters.

case: Dubai/Sharjah Border Arbitration
parties: Emirate of Dubai v. Emirate of Sharjah
issue: Land boundary and the lateral maritime boundary between two emirates inside the UAE federation; role of British-era decisions and tribal allegiance.
outcome: Boundary fixed by the tribunal, including the sea boundary. Details to read.
how_checked: Existence and citation confirmed on Cambridge ILR. Date and contents from memory.
why_it_matters: Emirates within one federation settling sea limits by international arbitration. Shows that each emirate still holds its own coast, which matters for emirate-level marine reserves.

court: Ras Al Khaimah Court of Cassation, Criminal Division
case: Appeal No. 16 of Judicial Year 2
parties: Ship's master (name withheld) v. Public Prosecution
citation: RAK Cassation, Appeal 16/2 Q, session 21/10/2007 (9 Shawwal 1428)
arabic_title: الطعن 16 لسنة 2 ق جلسة 21 / 10 / 2007 تلويث البحر بالزيت
issue: Diesel spill during ship-to-ship transfer with Iranian launches, 21.8 nautical miles off Al Jazeera Al Hamra. Was the court competent outside the 12-mile territorial sea?
outcome: Appeal dismissed. The court held that the marine environment protected by Federal Law 24/1999 reaches the exclusive economic zone, and read UNCLOS articles 55-57, 192, 194, 211 and 220 to support this. First-instance penalty had been one year and AED 150,000.
how_checked: Full Arabic text read on the Ras Al Khaimah Public Prosecution portal.
why_it_matters: A national court uses UNCLOS to stretch its own penal reach to 200 miles. Clear example of a global treaty being absorbed into local criminal law. No Sharia reference in the reasoning, which is itself telling.
paper_section: 4 (law by decree and penalties); 6 (international law used at home)
colleague_check: yes - confirm reading of the Arabic text and the court's wording on the EEZ

case: Shrimp ban and bottom trawling (case number not given)
parties: Public Prosecution v. seven men (five Indian, two Bahraini)
issue: Fishing for shrimp during the seasonal ban with banned bottom trawl nets; tracking device switched off; no licence.
outcome: Ten days in prison each; the five foreign nationals deported; boats, nets and catch confiscated.
how_checked: News report (Daily Tribune). No judgment text.
why_it_matters: Typical of many Bahraini shrimp cases: short sentences, deportation of foreign crew, confiscation. Shows who carries the cost of conservation.

outcome: One year for the official, three months for the fisherman; upheld on appeal.

case: 'Organisation and Function of Salifah Court' (file 5/7)
parties: Correspondence of Charles Belgrave (Adviser to the Government of Bahrain) and the Political Agent
issue: The customary court that judged pearl-diving disputes (debts, shares, crew duties) under sawalif al-ghaus, and its reform in the late 1920s.
outcome: Archive file on its make-up and reform. Case records not yet read.
how_checked: Catalogue record on the Qatar Digital Library; the digitised file has not been read.
why_it_matters: The main local court of the sea before oil. Shows custom judged by sea people themselves, then reshaped by the state and British advisers. Key for continuity and heritage arguments.

case: Bahraini fishermen in Qatari waters (case number not given)

why_it_matters: Shows fishing grounds shared for generations becoming hard borders after Qatar v. Bahrain and the 2017 rift, and a plea for forgiveness shaping the sentence. Pairs with INT-01.
